job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I read the manager's amendment text against the questions you asked: what lets companies continue, what makes enforcement difficult, and what invites a legal challenge. Items that depend on existing law (the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, OCSLA, federal criminal venue and savings statutes) come from general knowledge, so counsel should confirm them before we cite them to staff.

## Section 2: Definitions

1. **§2(1)(A), single-vessel threshold.** The threshold applies per vessel, so a company can run several vessels, each under 10,000 tons, and none is "commercial deep seabed mining." Nothing aggregates vessels under common ownership or control, or across affiliates.

2. **§2(1)(A), measurement.** The text doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry weight, or whether it covers nodules alone or also sediment and water brought up with them. It also doesn't say how the amount is measured or verified, which creates room for disputes and under-reporting.

3. **§2(1)(A), "per year."** The period isn't defined as a calendar year, a rolling 12 months, or a license year. Operators could structure campaigns around the boundary, and a prosecutor would have trouble proving a violation.

4. **§2(1)(A), "recovery" and "mineral resources."** Neither term is defined. It is unclear whether the text reaches crusts, massive sulfides, phosphorites, rare-earth muds, or sediment plumes and tailings, or whether "recovery" covers only lifting material to the surface.

5. **§2(1)(A), the 200-meter line.** The text doesn't say how depth is measured (at the collector, the seabed, or the claim area), what datum applies, or how to treat sites that straddle the line. Shallower deposits are outside the definition altogether.

6. **§2(1)(A), the Act never defines "seabed" or its geographic scope.** There is no reference to the EEZ, the extended continental shelf, or areas beyond national jurisdiction. Reach over U.S. waters versus the high seas is left to inference.

7. **§2(1), activities other than recovery.** Test mining below the threshold, bulk sampling, at-sea processing, transport, and offloading aren't covered. A company can build out most of the supply chain without "recovering" more than the threshold.

8. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** The Act never defines "Secretary" for this section, and §6 uses it for the Secretary of State. It's unclear whether Commerce, Interior, or State makes the determination.

9. **§2(1)(B), discretionary determination.** There is no deadline, no criteria beyond "comparable" risk, no publication or notice requirement, and no duty to act. Criminal liability that turns on an unpublished agency determination invites vagueness and nondelegation challenges, and the provision may never be used in practice.

10. **§2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition covers citizens and State-organized corporations only. It leaves out foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. firms, LLCs, partnerships, trusts, D.C. and territorial entities, and permanent residents, and it has no control or ownership test.

11. **§2(3), "covered vessel."** The 5,000 gross ton floor and "equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources" leave out smaller vessels, barges, platforms, and stand-alone seabed collectors. "Equipped" is also undefined, so an operator could argue a vessel is only retrofitted for recovery when needed.

## Section 3: Prohibition

12. **§3(a), "engage in."** The text doesn't say whether financing, chartering vessels, supplying equipment, owning equity, or contracting with a foreign operator counts. Companies could structure around the ban through those roles.

13. **§3(a), scope of "in the United States."** It is unclear whether the phrase covers the EEZ, the outer continental shelf, or territories. The "U.S. person anywhere" clause doesn't cover foreign entities operating abroad, even with U.S. money or technology.

14. **§3, no limit on processing, import, or sale.** The Act doesn't restrict importing, processing, or selling seabed minerals recovered by foreign operators or by exempt operations. The market incentive for deep-sea mining stays in place.

15. **§3, relationship to existing law.** The Act doesn't amend or repeal the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, which authorizes NOAA exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits, and it doesn't address OCSLA minerals authority. Without a supremacy or "notwithstanding" clause, agencies might keep processing applications and issuing permits.

16. **§3(b), grandfathering is open-ended.** "Mining conducted under an exploration license" has no cap on volume, area, or duration, and it exempts commercial-scale recovery under a license that normally authorizes only exploration. It also doesn't address renewals, extensions, amendments, expansions, or transfers of the license.

17. **§3(b), "an exploration license issued before enactment."** The text doesn't say who must have issued the license. A license from a foreign government or the International Seabed Authority, held by a U.S. person, might qualify. It also creates an incentive to rush applications and issuances before enactment.

18. **§3(b), no compliance condition.** Nothing requires a grandfathered operator to stay in compliance with its license terms or with environmental conditions. Nothing lets the government revoke the exemption for violations.

19. **§3(c), the environmental assessment exemption turns on subjective "purpose."** It has no limit on scale, duration, equipment, or method, no definition of "environmental assessment," and no approval or oversight. Commercial-scale test mining could be labeled assessment, and mixed-purpose activity is unaddressed.

## Section 4: Registry

20. **§4, no enforcement hook.** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register or report carries no penalty. Nothing says false certifications fall under 18 U.S.C. 1001 or any specific provision.

21. **§4(a), no timing or content requirements.** There is no deadline to register, no registration contents, no update obligation, and no definition of "operator." Foreign-flag vessels operated by or for U.S. persons aren't clearly covered.

22. **§4(b), reports are thin.** The text doesn't require tonnage, location, mineral type, or depth. It doesn't set a filing deadline, require verification or inspection, or require vessel tracking, and the operator certifies its own report.

23. **§4, no agency authority or public access.** NOAA has no rulemaking mandate, no appropriation, and no stated public-disclosure rule. The data can't clearly be used for public monitoring or to support enforcement.

## Section 5: Penalties

24. **§5(a) and §8, retroactivity mismatch.** The civil penalty applies to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days later. That creates ambiguity about whether §3 applies during the gap, and it invites a due process or fair-notice challenge.

25. **§5, no enforcing agency or process.** The text doesn't designate an agency, and it doesn't say whether penalties are assessed administratively or sought in district court. There is no notice and hearing procedure, no statute of limitations, and no provision for injunctions.

26. **§5, no forfeiture or disgorgement.** The Act doesn't authorize seizing vessels, equipment, or recovered minerals, or recovering profits. A fine of up to $1,000,000 per day may be treated as a cost of doing business by a large operator.

27. **§5, no liability for facilitators.** The text doesn't address aiding and abetting, corporate officers, or parent companies. It also doesn't say how "each day" counts for continuing operations.

28. **§5(b), venue and extraterritoriality.** Conduct on the high seas may fall under the general venue statute (18 U.S.C. 3238), but the Act doesn't say so or state its extraterritorial intent expressly. "Willfully" is also undefined for corporate defendants.

29. **§5, no citizen suit or whistleblower provision.** Enforcement depends entirely on agency discretion and resources. Outside parties can't compel enforcement.

## Section 6: International agreement

30. **§6, weak mandate.** "Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" doesn't say whether the deadline applies to starting talks, concluding them, or ratifying. There are no consequences for missing it, no reporting to Congress, and no definition of "equivalent." There is also no link to ISA processes or to trade or diplomatic leverage.

## Section 7: Duration

31. **§7(a) versus §7(b), internal contradiction.** §7(a) says the ban lasts until Congress finds mining can be done safely, but §7(b) ends the whole Act after 10 years regardless. The ban therefore expires automatically, and the §7(a) protection is meaningless.

32. **§7(b), sunset runs from enactment.** Combined with the 180-day delay, the ban is in effect for roughly 9.5 years. The text has no savings clause for violations committed before the sunset, and it is unclear whether the general savings statute (1 U.S.C. 109) covers expiration rather than repeal.

33. **§7(a), vague standard and no process.** "Without serious harm" is undefined, and the NAS has no required deadline, scope, or findings. Once the ban lifts, no permitting or environmental regime is in place. The Act doesn't say whether lifting is partial or conditional.

34. **§7(b), investor signal.** A fixed 10-year horizon lets companies and financiers plan to wait out the ban. It weakens the deterrent effect on investment and licensing decisions today.

## Section 8: Effective date

35. **§8, 180-day gap.** Operators can ramp up, secure financing, or move into positions that give rise to reliance or takings arguments. Whether anything done in the gap is grandfathered depends on the ambiguities in items 16, 17, and 24.

## Structural and cross-cutting

36. **No findings or purpose section.** The bill doesn't state its constitutional basis (Commerce, Property, or Treaty power), the congressional findings, or its purposes. That weakens the defense against challenges and gives courts less guidance on ambiguities.

37. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes one provision, such as the §2(1)(B) delegation, the rest of the Act could be put at risk.

38. **No rulemaking authority or lead agency.** No agency is clearly responsible for regulations, guidance, or coordination. The Act authorizes no appropriations.

39. **No judicial review or standing provisions.** The text doesn't address who can challenge agency determinations or enforcement choices, or how.

40. **International-law exposure.** The Act doesn't address operators with foreign-flag vessels who invoke high-seas freedoms. Jurisdiction rests on nationality, which is why the narrow "U.S. person" definition (item 10) matters so much.

## Most serious problems

If you need to prioritize for the markup, I'd lead with these:

- The §7(a)/§7(b) contradiction (31).
- The open-ended §3(b) grandfather clause (16, 17).
- The §3(c) exemption (19).
- The §2(1)(A) single-vessel and measurement gaps (1, 2).
- The narrow "U.S. person" definition (10).
- The §5(a)/§8 effective-date mismatch (24).
- The registry having no enforcement mechanism (20).
- Unclear relationship to existing seabed-minerals law (15).

I can draft amendment language for any of these, or a one-page markup memo for committee staff.
